title: Mara and the Hymn
premise: Quentin Okafor, a late-night radio host whose call-in show has begun receiving voices from listeners who died the week before, returns to his grandmother's house after her funeral and finds that every photograph of the family now includes an empty wooden chair that wasn't there before. The chair appears in more pictures each night, and when the count reaches the number of living relatives, each person pictured will be claimed by whatever has been waiting in the house's foundations for four generations. As Quentin races to get his fractured family out, he learns his grandmother made a bargain to protect them all, and that the debt has come due in his voice. In the end Quentin takes his grandmother's place in the chair, broadcasting the hymn that binds the entity, saving his family but becoming the next voice on the line.
about_author: Cyrus Delacroix is the pen name of a former overnight radio producer who spent years logging calls from strangers at 3 a.m. and swears half of them were wrong about being alive. They write horror from a farmhouse in Vermont where the photographs, they note cheerfully, are all normal.

chapters.title: The Last Caller
chapters.summary: Quentin, hosting the overnight show, takes a call from a woman he's certain died in a car crash last Tuesday; her voice is calm, asking about a chair. Shaken, he plays it off as a prank on air. The emotional beat is the first crack in his decade-long armor of rational explanations, and the dread of realizing his audience heard it too.

chapters.title: Grandmother's House
chapters.summary: After his grandmother's funeral, Quentin returns to the family house to help his sister Adaeze sort the estate. The house smells of hymnals and dust; a wooden chair sits in the parlor that no one remembers owning. POV shifts between Quentin and Adaeze's wary grief. The beat is unease disguised as family obligation.

chapters.title: One Chair, Every Picture
chapters.summary: Sorting photo albums, Quentin finds the same plain wooden chair in every image—weddings, christenings, 1970s barbecues—always empty, always slightly closer to the camera. Adaeze insists the chair was always there; Quentin knows it wasn't. The beat is gaslight-adjacent horror as memory itself becomes untrustworthy.

chapters.title: The Hymn in the Walls
chapters.summary: At night, Quentin hears faint singing through the floorboards—an old hymn his grandmother hummed, sung in a voice with too many throats. He records it and plays it on air; a listener calls in sobbing, saying she heard her dead mother singing harmony. The beat is the horror going public, no longer containable.

chapters.title: Adaeze's Denial
chapters.summary: Adaeze, protective of her children, accuses Quentin of manufacturing scares to avoid grief. A family dinner collapses when her son Marcus quietly asks why the chair in the photos keeps moving nearer. The beat is loyalty weaponized: the family closes ranks against the truth-teller.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Ledger
chapters.summary: In the attic, Quentin finds his grandmother's ledger: names, dates, and a column labeled 'seats.' Each generation's count matches deaths in the family—and the final page has his name, dated weeks away. The beat is the cold clarity of inheritance as a contract he never signed.

chapters.title: The Second Chair
chapters.summary: A second chair appears in the photographs, beside the first. Adaeze finally sees it and goes silent. Marcus begins sleepwalking toward the parlor each night. The beat is Adaeze's conversion from skeptic to believer, and the terrible intimacy of shared fear.

chapters.title: Callers Who Aren't Done
chapters.summary: Quentin's show is flooded with calls from the recently dead, all asking the same question: 'How many chairs now?' His station manager threatens to fire him as clips go viral. The beat is Quentin's public identity and private terror fusing—he can no longer hide behind the microphone.

chapters.title: What Grandma Sang
chapters.summary: A neighbor, Mrs. Okonkwo, reveals that Quentin's grandmother used to lead a hymn circle that 'kept the house fed'—and that she stopped singing after her husband's death, buying the family ten quiet years. The beat is the revelation that protection was always a transaction.

chapters.title: The Third Chair
chapters.summary: Three chairs now, and Marcus has begun humming the hymn in his sleep. Adaeze tries to burn the photo albums; the chair appears in new photographs taken that same day, including her phone. The beat is the futility of destroying evidence of something that lives in the seeing.

chapters.title: Family Meeting
chapters.summary: Quentin gathers the surviving family—Adaeze, her husband Theo, Marcus, and their estranged uncle Ray—to show them the ledger. Ray admits he left the family decades ago because he saw the chair take their grandfather. The beat is truth fracturing loyalty: some would rather flee than know.

chapters.title: Ray's Testimony
chapters.summary: Ray recounts the night in 1985 when the chairs equaled the family and their grandfather simply wasn't there anymore—no body, no goodbye, just an extra voice in the walls. The beat is grief reframed; every family tragedy was a payment, and Quentin's childhood losses recontextualized.

chapters.title: Evacuation
chapters.summary: The family packs to leave, but the house resists: roads loop back, phones show the parlor in every camera, and Marcus refuses to go, saying the singing is 'nicer than home.' The beat is the horror that the entity doesn't hold them by force but by want.

chapters.title: The Count Reaches Four
chapters.summary: Four chairs in every photograph. Theo, a rational man, breaks and flees alone; his car is found empty on the highway, radio tuned to Quentin's frequency. The beat is the cost of disbelief, and Quentin's guilt for telling the truth that shattered Theo's certainty.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Recording
chapters.summary: Quentin finds a reel-to-reel tape of his grandmother singing the full hymn, with a spoken coda: 'It takes a voice that loves them to call them home. Sing it wrong and it takes the singer instead.' The beat is hope with a hook—the cure is also the trap.

chapters.title: Learning the Hymn
chapters.summary: Quentin and Adaeze study the tape; the hymn is a naming-song, each verse a family member's true name, and it must be sung without error or hesitation. Marcus, disturbingly, already knows every verse. The beat is dawning horror that the child is being prepared as a replacement singer.

chapters.title: The Fifth Chair
chapters.summary: Five chairs. The walls sing louder; Mrs. Okonkwo is found in her kitchen, gone, her radio playing the hymn. Quentin realizes the entity is accelerating, harvesting the extended family to force his hand. The beat is the shift from haunting to siege.

chapters.title: What Marcus Knows
chapters.summary: Marcus confesses the singing voice told him he was chosen to 'keep the family together forever,' and that Grandma promised him the house. Adaeze must choose between her son's safety and the truth that he's already half-claimed. The beat is maternal loyalty at war with truth.

chapters.title: The Bargain Reversed
chapters.summary: Quenton confronts the entity in the parlor at 3 a.m., offering himself in Marcus's place. The chairs rearrange to face him; the voice that answers uses his grandmother's timbre, then his own. The beat is the seduction of power—the entity offers him the show's true purpose: a voice that calls the dead.

chapters.title: The Broadcast
chapters.summary: Quentin hijacks his own radio show, broadcasting live from the parlor, and sings the hymn—every name but his own—binding the entity to the house and freeing the claimed voices. The chairs empty one by one on air as thousands listen. The beat is triumph laced with sacrifice: the final verse remains unsung.

chapters.title: The Empty Chair
chapters.summary: The family flees at dawn; the house stands silent, photographs clean. But in every picture taken since, there is one chair—empty, waiting—and Marcus hums a new final verse he says Quentin taught him. The beat is bittersweet victory: the debt is deferred, not erased.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: Epilogue: Quentin's show airs one last time, his voice calm as he takes a final call—from himself, ten years younger, asking about a chair. He signs off with the hymn's last verse and the line goes quiet. The beat is acceptance: he chose the chair, and the chair, at last, chose to let him sing.
